title: the Tao: those who know they have enough are rich
hookLine: the Tao: those who know they have enough are rich

lines: THE GLOW, THEN THE NEXT THING.
A PARTY GIVEN BY A BILLIONAIRE.
cards: The shoes arrive. Or the phone, or the upgrade. For a few days there's a glow.

Then, often, it's just a thing that's owned, and the wanting has already moved on to the next one. Kurt Vonnegut told a story about this. He and his fellow novelist Joseph Heller were at a party given by a billionaire.
Vonnegut pointed out that their host might have made more in a single day than Heller's best-known novel had earned in its whole life.
Heller said he had something the billionaire could never have: the knowledge that he had enough.

teach.h: SATISFIED WITH HIS LOT IS RICH.
teach.b: Heller was in old company. The Tao Te Ching, the short Chinese classic traditionally credited to Lao-tzu, has a chapter of paired sayings about strength and knowledge.
In the middle of it, in an old translation: "He who is satisfied with his lot is rich." In the Chinese it's four characters, and the first two mean knowing enough. Not having enough.
Knowing it. Richness, in this picture, isn't a number in a bank account. It's a kind of recognition.

teach.h: THE POOR ONE KEEPS CRAVING MORE.
teach.b: The Roman Stoic Seneca made the same turn in a letter to a friend: the poor person isn't the one who has too little, but the one who keeps craving more.
And the Greek philosopher Epicurus, whose name now gets attached to fine dining, is reported to have been content with bread and water, and to have prized friendship above almost anything.
Modern psychologists have a name for what all three were pushing against: the hedonic treadmill. When we get something we wanted, we get used to it, fast, and our sense of normal moves up.
So the chase never finishes, because the finish line walks away as we approach it. Knowing enough doesn't mean you stop wanting anything or never improve your life.

teach.h: STEP OFF, AND SAY THE WORD.
teach.b: It means that now and then you step off the treadmill and say the word. The traditions that teach it don't promise it'll make you rich. They say it's what rich actually is.

how: Contentment is practiced on several paths: Taoists speak of knowing enough, Stoics and Epicureans practiced living simply, and some people keep a habit of pausing to name what they already have.

games.q: who said enough — tap the pairs.
p: satisfied with his lot is rich
the poor one keeps craving more
we get used to things, fast

s: Epicurus taught a life of feasting and excess
he's reported to have been content with bread and water, and he prized friendship.
in the Chinese, the Tao Te Ching's line is about knowing enough
the first two characters mean knowing enough. not having it: knowing it.
knowing enough means never wanting anything again
it means stepping off the treadmill now and then and saying the word.

games.q: you're Joseph Heller at a billionaire's party, and a friend says your host may have made more in a day than your novel ever did. what do you say?
o: that you'll catch up one day.
that you have something he can never have: knowing you have enough.
nothing. you go home and write another book.
games.why: in Vonnegut's telling, Heller says he has the knowledge that he's got enough. the Tao Te Ching's line, too, is about knowing enough.

practice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. For about forty-five seconds, let your eyes or your mind move over what you have right now.
Not the whole house, just what's in reach. The chair holding you up. The clothes you're wearing.
The breath coming in without being asked. For each one, say inside: enough. Not forever.

wordCard.voice: Enough. Not having it: knowing it. The quiet partner to every vision board. Thirteenth word.

orig.note: Chinese, zhī zú, from the Tao Te Ching 33: knowing enough, being content. The line reads, word for word, knowing-enough-one rich.

carryVoice: Your line: enough. The one thing in the story the billionaire couldn't buy. Day thirteen.
